11: Tip: Don't try to learn “general English” first. Start with the technical word, see it in real code or in an error message you actually got, then memorize it. Words you meet in context stick faster than words from a list. And say every word out loud at least once.
12: Start with the intensive week: 7 days, about two hours a day, where you learn to read error messages and docs, write commits, READMEs and bug reports, ask and reply professionally, and pronounce technical terms correctly. Then continue with the 12-week plan (40 minutes a day) to lock it in and become fluent at work.
26: Honestly: one week won't make you fluent. But it will get you reading error messages and docs without translating, and writing correct technical English at work (commits, READMEs, emails and questions) — exactly the English developers use every day. Fluency comes with the daily plan over months.
27: Pick an answer and you'll see right away whether it's right or wrong, and why. Questions you get wrong show up in the “The ones I got wrong” tab, so come back to them after a day.

47: The shape of an error message
48: Most error messages share the same shape: the error type, a colon, then a short description. Read the type first — it tells you the category.
49: A traceback is read from the bottom up
50: The last line is the error itself, and the lines above it are the path the code took until it failed. Look for the first line that mentions your own file.
51: Words that keep appearing in errors
52: expected (what it wanted), got (what arrived), missing, invalid, unexpected, not found, denied (refused), out of range (beyond the limits), deprecated (old and going away).
54: Error = something stopped the program. Warning = a caution, and the program carried on. Exception = a run-time error you can “catch” with try/except.

57: raise/throw = produce an error. catch/handle = grab the error and deal with it. fail. crash = stop suddenly. hang/freeze = get stuck. time out = run out of time.

102: Open any docs page and quickly find what you need: what the function takes, what it returns, and which error it may raise.
103: The structure of a docs page
104: Most docs pages share the same sections: Description, Parameters (inputs), Returns (output), Raises (errors), Example, and Note or Warning.
105: Docs are written in the present simple
106: That's why verbs end in s: returns, takes, raises, accepts. It's the same style you should write in.
108: It focuses on what happened, not on who did it: is + the verb's third form (V3).
110: optional, required, default, if omitted (if not provided), must, should, may.
112: Note = extra important information. Warning = a danger, or something that could lose data. Tip = advice. Deprecated since = old since version X.
114: Don't read the whole docs page. Read the first sentence, then Parameters and Returns, then the example. If it's still unclear, go back to the description.

149: Function names start with a verb
150: A function does something, so its name starts with a verb: get, set, fetch, load, save, parse, validate, convert, handle, send, build, calculate.
151: Variables are nouns; booleans are questions
152: A variable is a noun (user, orders, total_price). True/False values start with is, has, can or should.
